transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-09
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~74 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Evan Chen (Redwood SE), Tom Alvarez (Lucida ML Infra), Priya Singh (Platform Eng), Rachel Kim (Security), Alex Duong (SRE), Jorge Martinez (Data Science)

[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll give a quick agenda, then dive into the benchmarking playbook and make sure we have an apples-to-apples protocol for on-prem lab runs and eventual pilot. Evan and I will lead; feel free to jump in.
[00:12] Tom Alvarez: Thanks Maya. Big goal: we need to validate latency and cost tradeoffs on our on-prem racks before committing to dedicated cloud capacity. We also need a repeatable methodology for procurement.
[00:25] Evan Chen: Great. We'll cover prompt normalization, load shapes, KV cache priming, batching, and quant profiles. Also network and KMS considerations for your VPC/on-prem setup.
[00:38] Priya Singh: Quick callout — our primary constraint is tail latency at 99.9% under 350ms for our chat feature. Throughput is important but tail is our blocker.
[00:50] Jorge Martinez: And quality — we can't accept more than a 2% drop measured by our rouge-like metric on the prompt set after quantization.
[01:02] Rachel Kim: Security question up front: we will need to see how keys are stored, rotation, audit logs, and whether Redwood's private deploy supports our HSM. SOC2 is table stakes.
[01:14] Maya Patel: All right noted — we'll show the KMS/HSM story and the audit artifacts in the security pack. For benchmarks let's start with the prompt set.
[01:20] 
[01:20] Evan Chen: Prompt sets — we recommend three tiers: micro (short queries, 8-32 tokens), standard (average user, 64-256 tokens), and long-context (1k+ tokens) matching your product mix. Jorge, does that reflect your telemetry?
[01:35] Jorge Martinez: Yes that's close. Our distribution is roughly 30% micro, 60% standard, 10% long-ish — but the long ones skew latency because of KV misses.
[01:48] Evan Chen: Important to normalize prompts for apples-to-apples runs: remove non-deterministic elements, fix temperature and sampling seeds, and include system messages consistently. We will provide a canonical prompt file.
[02:02] Tom Alvarez: When you say normalize, do you mean we mask user IDs and replace with placeholders?
[02:08] Evan Chen: Exactly. Replace anything tied to PII or dynamic context — but maintain semantic complexity. For quality checks we also preserve the answer key for reference prompts.
[02:18] 
[02:20] Maya Patel: Load generation — we propose three load profiles for lab runs: steady-state (sustained RPS at target throughput), spiky (bursts that emulate peak windows), and stress/burst (>2x for short bursts). We'll also run ramp tests to find knee points.
[02:36] Alex Duong: For steady-state, do you recommend arrival process Poisson? Our infra behaves more bursty; we can replay traces too.
[02:43] Evan Chen: Poisson arrival is a good baseline; we'll also use replay of your 48h traces to get realistic distribution. The key is to produce identical external load for each run — same seeds, same ordering.
[02:55] Priya Singh: How do you handle KV cache priming? In our system we rely on prefix caching to shave 15–30% off token cost sometimes.
[03:05] Evan Chen: We'll use two KV experiments: cold start (no cache primed) and warm start (repeat requests to reach steady hit-rate). We'll measure cache hit curve over time and correlate to token-level latency. Note that priming strategies can bias batching so we log batch sizes per request.
[03:20] Jorge Martinez: Do you have a recommended priming script? We can see issues where priming floods saturate GPU memory.
[03:26] Evan Chen: Yes — our harness includes a priming mode that steps up RPS gradually and monitors memory/KV miss rates. We also cap concurrent priming threads so it doesn't blow up memory. We'll share that script.
[03:36] 
[03:40] Maya Patel: On batching — Redwood runtime supports continuous batching; the key knobs are max batch size and max latency window. For on-prem labs we want to test several policy points: small batches for tight tail latency vs larger batches for cost efficiency.
[03:55] Tom Alvarez: How do you simulate real arrival concurrency? If we artificially coalesce requests, that creates unrealistic lower latency numbers.
[04:03] Evan Chen: Correct. That's why we emphasize request ordering and realistic inter-arrival times. The harness will replay the real trace and the runtime will batch naturally; we capture observed batch sizes and per-request latency so we can break down latency by batch size.
[04:17] Priya Singh: Are there standard metrics you recommend for comparison? P50/P95/P99/P999, tokens/sec, cost per 1k tokens, and quality deltas?
[04:25] Evan Chen: Yes — and add batch-size distribution, cache hit-rate, GPU utilization, memory footprint, and request-level tail latency aligned to batch size. We'll provide dashboards.
[04:36] 
[04:40] Jorge Martinez: Quantization matrix — we want to try 4-bit and 8-bit variants but need to prevent quality regressions. How do you propose measuring quality systematically?
[04:50] Evan Chen: We'll run side-by-side runs with the same seed and prompts. Metrics: embedding cosine for embedding tasks, generation BLEU/ROUGE-like metrics for fixed-answer prompts, and our custom hallucination heuristics. We'll compute relative deltas and flag anything >2% for manual review.
[05:05] Tom Alvarez: Also include temperature differences and sampling — quant can interact with sampling causing variance.
[05:11] Evan Chen: Agreed — we fix sampling seeds for deterministic comparators. For sampling-based evaluation we use a fixed set of top-k/top-p seeds.
[05:19] 
[05:20] Rachel Kim: On the security front, if we're running on-prem, we need to know what levels of admin access Redwood requires, whether logs are exfiltrated, and what the agent/containerization model looks like.
[05:30] Maya Patel: For private deployments Redwood provides a customer-controlled control plane option: data plane stays within your network; logs optionally forwarded to your SIEM. We'll give you an HLD and the packaging model (container image + operator). We support bringing-your-own-KMS and HSM integration.
[05:46] Rachel Kim: Do you produce audit logs for prompt-level access? We need immutable logs for e-discovery and audits.
[05:52] Evan Chen: Yes, per-request audit logs with configurable retention. We can also hook to your syslog or cloud logging endpoint.
[05:59] 
[06:00] Alex Duong: Network egress — our security team doesn't want outbound calls except to our internal registry. Are there components that phone home?
[06:07] Maya Patel: Only the optional telemetry/control plane. For air-gapped runs we can disable telemetry; operator will run fully offline. We'll provide instructions for image pulls and offline mirrors.
[06:18] 
[06:20] Evan Chen: Back to methodology — apples-to-apples rules: same model weights (no pruning), same tokenization, same temperature/seeds, same prompt normalization, and identical hardware configuration (GPU model, driver, CUDA/cuDNN versions). If any of these differ we annotate and treat as a separate experiment.
[06:38] Priya Singh: For hardware, we run on T4-like and A100 racks. Can Redwood runtime calibrate kernels differently based on GPU architecture? We don't want to compare apples to oranges.
[06:48] Evan Chen: The runtime chooses kernels per-device; in the protocol we insist to record kernel-versions and runtime flags. We also run cross-device sanity runs so differences are explicit.
[06:58] Jorge Martinez: What about mixed-precision and kernel fusion?
[07:02] Evan Chen: We'll include flags for FP16/FP32/fused ops in experiment metadata. All that metadata gets stored with each run.
[07:10] 
[07:12] Tom Alvarez: Let's talk about measurement noise. Even on identical runs we see variance. How many repeats do you recommend?
[07:18] Evan Chen: We run each experiment at least 5 times and compute mean and standard deviation; for tail metrics we recommend 10 runs or longer steady-state runs (10 minutes+) to get stable 99.9th percentiles.
[07:29] Priya Singh: For cost modeling, do you provide tokenized cost extrapolations? We need to map tokens/sec to monthly spend on dedicated capacity.
[07:36] Maya Patel: Yes — Redwood Optimize will produce cost per million tokens using your run metrics and assumed concurrency. For on-prem we provide a per-hour GPU cost model you can substitute with your internal accounting.
[07:47] 
[07:50] Evan Chen: A small demo of the harness — (screen share noise) — the harness collects per-request latency, batch size, kv hit, gpu util, memory and saves to a CSV and a JSON run artifact. It also supports priming mode.
[08:05] Priya Singh: That demo was a bit fuzzy on screen. Can you share the repo link?
[08:09] Maya Patel: We'll share the repo and runbook after the call.
[08:13] 
[08:15] Jorge Martinez: A question on KV semantics: if we change the cache key scheme between models, hits drop. How do you ensure the keying is consistent across runs?
[08:23] Evan Chen: We log the exact keying algorithm per run and provide deterministic key generation utility in the harness. For on-prem we can also snapshot the KV store before and after runs.
[08:33] 
[08:35] Alex Duong: Any guidance on priming frequency in production vs lab? In prod we prime incrementally; in the lab we tend to over-prime and get unrealistic hit curves.
[08:43] Evan Chen: Priming should emulate your warm-up windows. Use a priming ramp equal to your 95th percentile session length; don't fully populate the KV unless your production does. We'll help tune that based on your traces.
[08:56] 
[09:00] Tom Alvarez: Regarding quantization: we worry about calibration artifacts causing latency regressions. Do you have a way to correlate quantization-induced accuracy loss to latency gains?
[09:09] Evan Chen: We'll produce pareto plots of tokens/sec vs quality delta and let you pick acceptable operating points. Also include memory footprint and effective max concurrency.
[09:21] Rachel Kim: Re SOC2/ISO: can you provide your SOC2 Type II evidence for the managed plane? For private deploy we expect a compliance pack.
[09:31] Maya Patel: We'll include SOC2 artifacts for hosted control plane and a checklist for what we provide in private deploy. For any missing audited items we will document compensating controls.
[09:42] 
[09:45] Evan Chen: A few gotchas from prior pilots: 1) tokenization mismatches between toolchains; 2) priming that overwhelms GPU memory; 3) ignoring batch-size distribution when reporting average latency. We'll include a pitfalls doc.
[09:58] Jorge Martinez: Good. Also note that some compilers produce non-deterministic kernel timings depending on env variables — we need the environment snapshot.
[10:08] Evan Chen: All experiment env variables, driver versions, and runtime flags are captured.
[10:12] 
[10:15] Maya Patel: Let's map next steps and owners. Evan will package the harness and quant scripts. I'll send a runbook and example dashboards. Tom you'll provide traces. Rachel you'll review the security checklist.
[10:28] Tom Alvarez: Sounds good. On the pilot lab — what does Redwood need from us network-wise?
[10:33] Maya Patel: Access to a bastion for image pulls OR an offline image bundle, plus a service account with limited privilege to create k8s namespaces and view resource usage. No blanket admin required. We'll provide exact RBAC roles.
[10:45] Priya Singh: Are there licensing or EULA items that block us from running this in our air-gapped environment?
[10:52] Maya Patel: The operator supports air-gapped installs; we'll include the license text. Our legal team can have a quick sync if needed.
[10:59] 
[11:00] Jorge Martinez: Timing — if we can provide traces this week, when can we expect the first lab report?
[11:06] Evan Chen: If we get traces by 2026-07-16, we can run baseline 1 and send initial results by 2026-07-23. The detailed quant matrix would follow the week after.
[11:17] Tom Alvarez: That's acceptable.
[11:20] 
[11:20] Rachel Kim: One more — do you support bringing your own model weights or only Redwood-curated model variants?
[11:27] Evan Chen: For private deployments you can bring your own weights; we'll help onboard them. For hosted we host curated weights only. We'll document the onboarding checklist.
[11:36] 
[11:40] Maya Patel: Recap of decisions: canonical prompt set and normalization rules; three load profiles and replay-based runs; priming modes (cold/warm) with priming scripts; quantization matrix and deterministic seeds; full environment metadata capture; security checklist and KMS/HSM options.
[11:56] Priya Singh: Agreed. We'll send a short acceptance criteria doc with our 99.9 latency target and <2% quality delta limit.
[12:05] Maya Patel: Great — we'll align against that. Any final questions?
[12:10] Alex Duong: Not from SRE side.
[12:12] Jorge Martinez: No.
[12:14] Tom Alvarez: Thanks everyone.
[12:16] Maya Patel: Thanks — we'll follow up with the repo, runbook, and schedule pilot kickoff.
[12:20] (Recording ends)
